evidence.quote: Really looking forward to covering how and why and the methodology around what we know at LangChain to be about owning your own intelligence.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And so we did this at LangChain recently.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: This is an iterative process, but really a way that we found to do this quite successfully at LangChain, and again, this is something that's constantly evaluating, is through the idea of working with specifications to define the agent's world as well as the tasks within it.

entities.name: 智能体 (agent)
entities.how_described: 本集主线：构建智能体要能回答三个问题——它在哪里出错、怎么让错误稳定重现、怎么让它以后不再错

evidence.quote: I'm going to approach what it means to own your own intelligence from a practitioner's angle for someone who's building with agents and for someone who is probably going through a lot of the processes that it takes that I'm about to cover when it comes to building and improving your agent.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: I think that there are three main questions that any person who's building an agent needs to have a very solid grasp of.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: So that starts with when you're building agents, understanding what goes wrong and understanding where your agent fails.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: This is obviously a very, you know, this is a simple question, but actually there's a lot of engineering work that goes into understanding if an agent failed.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: I think to answer the first question and to understand really how and why your agent has failed requires a very strong grasp of tracing and understanding your agent's behavior.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And this often comes from mining your agent's production traces.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: Building an agent, hopefully you're tracing it.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: You're gonna have a lot of trajectories and understandings of all of the different kinds of behavior that your agent is taking.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: that you can use to move on the path to improving your agent.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: That might be, for example, times where the agent either successfully called a tool or it incorrectly called a tool.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: There's a variety of different signal within your agent traces, particularly your production traces, that is a very important element to capture when it comes to owning your own intelligence and understanding whether or not your agent failed.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: The issue with doing that at scale, obviously, is that if you have an agent that has thousands of runs a day, millions of runs a day, it's going to be very hard to understand at scale whether or not your agent is performing as you expect it to.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And so as an example, a way that we approach this and just one of the ways that you can look towards understanding and extracting signal from your agent traces
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: is by making evaluation specific judges to go and extract and actually mine your agent for production signal.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: We worked with fine tuning, labeling, and producing a judge to go and actually classify whether or not an agent was giving users a delightful experience, whether or not there was any perceived error.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: So that might be, for example, an agent frustrating user or it might be a string of tool calls that an agent makes that actually leads it to performing the wrong action when a user was looking for it to do something else.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And so being able to actually have some form of monitoring and understanding what your agent's doing at scale is a very important step towards understanding whether or not it failed.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And also a very important way to be able to cluster the behaviors and the failure mechanisms that begin to emerge as you build and as you start to improve your agent.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: This is only the first step in the journey though, because once we know and once we have classified agent behaviors, we then need to go and take a variety of next steps to go and be able to reproduce and then actually remediate these issues as they continue to develop.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: Where your agent is failing.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: The typical way of doing this, and actually rather the shallow way of looking at this, is just evaluating whether or not the inputs or evaluating whether or not the outputs to your agent, given some simple input produces the behavior that you expect.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: This is very powerful for capturing a variety of different agent failure mechanisms, but often doesn't encapsulate the full picture.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: The reason why is an agent's behavior might be influenced by external factors of the environment that it's in.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And so what we really need then is a way for us to be able to mock out the broader application machinery of your agent as it stands in production.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And that brings me to building more robust evaluations by creating a way where we can mimic the world or the environment that your agent exists in.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: This is an iterative process, but really a way that we found to do this quite successfully at LangChain, and again, this is something that's constantly evaluating, is through the idea of working with specifications to define the agent's world as well as the tasks within it.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: which defines the things that don't mutate across that agent's world.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And so that might be things like the permissions, or that might be like the domain-specific rules that an agent has access to, or that might be things like the state of the file system and the dependencies that it interacts with.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: This is things that don't change across the agent's actions that it takes in this action space.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: So an example of this is we have a very commonly used internal agent at LangChain.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: It's called the GTM agent.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: The world in that case would be all of the systems that the agent needs to interact with, Gong, Salesforce, Google Calendar, and effectively the systems that it touches and interacts with as this agent interacts and is engaged with by all of our sellers.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: Tasks within that world represent specific actions or tasks that the agent needs to take, which will go and actually test and hopefully surface different emergent behaviors and things you're trying to test for.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And so a task within that go-to-market agent world, for example, would be go and research all of the Gong transcripts for a particular customer that we're looking to investigate or are in the process of working with and help me draft a next best reach out.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And so if I'm someone who's building an environment or a place where I can reliably test my go-to-market agent in production, I'm probably going to want to have some concept of a robust world where it mimics the environment that that agent is operating with in production.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: One thing that we've noticed though, when kind of going and creating these worlds and developing these specs and working with an agent, a coding agent side by side to actually go and develop these.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And so something that's obviously very important in all of this is to make sure that the tasks that your agent is defining are both reliably hard and actually present a challenge for you to be able to continuously improve your agent with.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And also there aren't methods where the agent has designed tasks that are easy to reward hack.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: This is obviously really important as well because it makes sure that the world that we're developing and the tasks that we're giving our agent are sufficiently hard so that when we make improvements, they are quantifiable and actually mimic really what the agent would be doing in production.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And once we have this kind of like mechanism now of knowing that the way for us to really kind of get a handle on our own intelligence and be able to create and develop an agent that is solving problems in a world that actually mimics the world that it's the kind of environment that it's operating in.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: is that we have the ability to go and do this through turning that data that we have from monitoring our agent in production into these kinds of tasks, into these kinds of worlds.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And for that reason, they're able to produce data from their telemetry or they're able to understand how real people are actually interacting with and using their agent and therefore develop tasks and develop environments that a Frontier Lab never could.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: Once we know that from the traces of our agent, from all of this exhaust, from all of this substrate, we can really help design powerful tasks and worlds to be able to go in and actually help improve our agent, then obviously we know that it's a data wrangling problem because there's going to need to be deduplication.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: But once we do, we have the substrate and we have the foundation for a lot of further agent improvement and development.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And really then we have a strong benchmark and starting point for us to be able to go and actually make quantitative agent improvements.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And so once we have a world, once we have a set of tasks within that world, ideally a task targets some kind of failure mode that you've seen in your agent, right?
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: You would design tasks around where you've observed your production traffic or you've observed your production agent to be failing.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: Changes at the harness level might involve simple changes like prompts or tool schema changes or changing the way that context is injected so that an agent given a certain task can answer in a certain way.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: The environment and the agent running in that environment can pass those particular tasks and then begin to behave as we expect it to.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: It's inevitable that as models develop, parts of what we test for will change and regressions will be introduced, but also parts of what we designed for to solve for particular deficiencies in our agent will be absorbed as part of the model.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: But we'll be able to test for it because we now have a robust way to actually simulate how our agent is behaving in production.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: Also what will be also as well the interaction patterns of people using your agent will obviously change and having a strong way to be able to go and test and actually roll out and determine whether or not your agent holds up under those particular interaction patterns will still be available given that we have this really robust and powerful way to now test it.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

entities.name: 测试框架 (harness)
entities.how_described: 本集说框架层指模型外层的工程代码，改进可以在这一层改提示词、工具 schema、上下文注入方式，而长任务分解、动态工具路由等功能会不断被吸收进模型层

evidence.quote: This is obviously key on the process to being able to build agents that improve and to be able to own all parts of your model and maybe your harness and then the weights as well.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And this is really where owning your own intelligence and owning the mechanisms around both the harness and the models that are powering your agents really begins to compound because now you can have full flexibility to make changes at all levels here.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: Changes at the harness level might involve simple changes like prompts or tool schema changes or changing the way that context is injected so that an agent given a certain task can answer in a certain way.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00

evidence.quote: And I think that this is kind of no surprise to anyone, but we've constantly seen parts of the harness, whether it's a long task decomposition or whether it's dynamic tool routing be absorbed into the model layer.
evidence.speaker: SPEAKER_00
